Starting Clean: How to Begin an R Project You Can Trust

A two-hour standalone toolero session

RCI
reproducibility
research workflows
Author
Affiliation

Erwin Lares

Research Cyberinfrastructure (RCI), Division of Information Technology, UW-Madison

Published

October 7, 2026

0.1 What this session is about

Most researchers never deliberately learn renv, git, or how to keep a document and its code from drifting apart. Those habits get picked up in fragments, under deadline pressures, and usually only after something has already broken: a labmate can’t reproduce a figure, a script from three months ago won’t run, nobody remembers which package version produced the plot that is now in a manuscript. toolero exists so that adopting those habits doesn’t require becoming fluent in renv or git, or understanding how Quarto runs the code inside your document, before you can benefit from them.

This is a standalone, two-hour session covering toolero on its own terms: how to start a project, why to work in a literate document and when to run a plain script instead, how to keep the code in a document and in its script from drifting apart, and how to retrofit these habits onto something that already exists. It uses one running example throughout, bill and flipper measurements from the Palmer Penguins dataset, framed as data collected by a UW-Madison research team at Palmer Station.

0.2 Who this is for

This session assumes you’re comfortable writing R scripts and functions; dplyr, ggplot2, and basic data wrangling should feel familiar. It does not assume any prior experience with renv, git, or Quarto’s rendering model. If “reproducible project structure” is still a fairly abstract phrase to you, you’re exactly who this was built for.

0.3 What you’ll need

  • R (4.4.0 or later) and RStudio, recent versions. I built and tested this session in RStudio. Positron should work with little or no change; the places where it differs are mainly the metadata files RStudio creates when you work inside a Project

  • Quarto 1.4 or later (bundled with recent RStudio and Positron releases)

  • The toolero package, installed from GitHub until the current version reaches CRAN:

    install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("erwinlares/toolero")

  • readr, ggplot2, and rmarkdown, installed as usual (RStudio usually installs rmarkdown for you; Quarto needs it to render a document with R code in it)

  • A git installation, so that init_project()’s git initialization takes effect (optional, but the session is smoother with it)

  • This lesson open in your browser, next to your editor

  • One CSV file, palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv, which you will download at the start of Task 1. It stands in for “the data you already have”

0.4 Learning objectives

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

  • Identify the organizational decisions (file location, dependency tracking, version control) that quietly determine whether a project is (more) reproducible
  • Use init_project() to scaffold a new R project with a standard folder structure, renv, git, and a _toolero.yml record of its layout, in one call
  • Explain why a .qmd document, with prose and code together, can serve as a single source of truth
  • Explain how a render session differs from an interactive one: a render creates every object the analysis uses, in order, whereas an interactive session may unwittingly introduce objects that nothing in the document created
  • Explain why an unattended run, such as a pipeline or a cluster job, is better served by a plain .R script than by rendering a document
  • Use create_qmd() to scaffold a literate document whose YAML header is pre-populated from a profile you write once with generate_profile()
  • Explain what the purl hook (create_qmd(use_purl = TRUE)) does and where it stops protecting you: it fires on render, and the script it writes is output, not something to edit; and use check_project() to catch a script that has fallen behind its document
  • Recognize why one document can disagree with itself about where its data lives when it runs interactively, under quarto render, and under Rscript
  • Use resolve_input_path() to let one document find its input in all three contexts, and apply it to a document you have already written
  • Write every other path in code from the project root with here::here(), and explain why that keeps a document in reports/ from writing its results to the wrong place
  • Use save_output() and generate_manifest() to leave a record of what an analysis produced, and read it back with read_output_records()
  • Describe what minimal-project.qmd does, which kinds of research tasks it covers, and why it is the starting point for the next session
  • Use check_project() to audit a project against the checklist init_project() satisfies, and know that qmd_to_r() brings the purl habit to a document that didn’t start with create_qmd()

1 Part One: Starting a Project

1.1 Welcome and backdrop

You’re a postdoc who recently joined Dr. Maris Sphen’s research team at UW-Madison. The lab has spent the last several seasons at Palmer Station measuring bill and flipper dimensions across three penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo) as part of an ongoing study of morphological variation on the peninsula. Today you’re picking up where the lab’s fieldwork left off.

1.2 Task 1: the impromptu ask

It’s Tuesday afternoon. Maris is finishing a grant proposal due Friday and stops by your desk with palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv: “Can you put together a quick figure from this? Bill length against bill depth, colored by species. I just need something for the appendix.” You open your laptop and get to it.

1.2.1 Task

First, download the data: palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv. On that page, use the download button (Download raw file) and save it wherever you normally would.

Using palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv, produce a scatterplot of bill length against bill depth, colored by species. Work however you normally would. You have about eight minutes.

CautionShow me the answer

There’s no single correct way to do this; that is the point of the activity, not a gap in it. A straightforward version looks something like this:

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins <- read_csv("palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Bill Length vs. Bill Depth by Species",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)"
  )

This is one reference version among many equally valid ones. The variety across the room is exactly what the poll is about to surface.

1.3 Poll 1

Please answer the following poll:
https://go.wisc.edu/529dua

  1. Where on your computer did the .csv file end up, and where did your script end up? (Same folder / Different folders / I’m not entirely sure)
  2. Did you know, before this poll, which version of R or which package versions you’re running? (Yes / No / I didn’t think about it)
  3. If your laptop died right now, could you reconstruct this figure from what’s saved elsewhere? (Fully / Partially / Not really)
  4. Right now, could someone else in this room open your folder and know where to start? (Yes / Somewhat / No)
  5. What kind of file is your Task 1 code in right now? (An .R script / A .qmd or .Rmd document / Just the console / Something else)
  6. Thinking about analyses you have shared or rerun: do you keep both a document or notebook and a separate script of the same work? (Yes, and they have drifted apart / Yes, and I keep them in sync by hand / No, just one of the two)

1.3.1 Debrief and transition

Notice that nobody did anything careless. Where you saved the CSV, which packages you loaded, how you named your script: every choice was reasonable in the moment. That’s exactly the problem. It’s a long chain of small, sensible-in-the-moment decisions, oftentimes made without the luxury of thinking about the longevity of your work.

Hold that thought. Maris is about to come back with a second ask, and this one won’t be a five-minute favor.

1.4 Task 2: assume continuity

The grant is funded. Maris now wants this analysis built out properly, since it’s going to get rerun and extended over the life of the award. This isn’t a one-off figure anymore. It’s a project you’ll be coming back to for the next few years.

1.4.1 Task

Using whatever tools you’d normally reach for: (1) create a project folder for this analysis and initialize it with renv; (2) put it under git version control; (3) organize things however you’d want to find them again in six months. You have about eight minutes.

1.5 Poll 2

Please answer the following poll:
https://go.wisc.edu/228tv0

  1. How long did the folder-plus-renv-plus-git setup actually take you? (Under 2 minutes / 2–5 minutes / More than 5 minutes / Didn’t finish)
  2. Are you confident your renv setup captured what this analysis depends on? (Yes / Not sure / No)
  3. Did you set up git, commit as you went, both, or neither? (Set up and committed / Set up but didn’t commit / Skipped it entirely)
  4. If you had to do this again tomorrow for a new project, how much of it could you reuse versus redo from scratch? (Most of it / Some of it / Basically none)

1.5.1 Debrief

1.6 toolero’s answer: init_project() and create_qmd()

init_project() answers both of the tasks you’ve just done in a single call, and not only Task 2. It would have answered Task 1 just as readily:

CautionShow me the call 
library(toolero)

init_project(path = "~/Documents/palmer-morphometrics")

By default this creates a standard research-project folder structure (data-raw/, data/, R/, scripts/, output/figures/, output/tables/, and reports/), initializes both renv and git, and writes two small files: _toolero.yml, which records the project’s folders and conventions, and .here, an empty file that marks this folder as the project’s root. Both renv and git are on by default. Compare this against how long the equivalent setup took by hand a few minutes ago.

There is never a version of “just a quick figure” too small for this, and that cuts against instinct. A five-minute favor doesn’t feel like it deserves project scaffolding. But init_project() costs seconds, not minutes, so the real question was never “should I set this up properly?” It was “do I know in advance which tasks will turn into two-year projects?” Usually one doesn’t. Maris didn’t either, until Friday’s proposal got funded.

Let’s take a first look at _toolero.yml now, because it will keep turning up. It is a few lines of plain YAML saying which folders this project has, where outputs go (output_dir), where derived scripts live (script_dir), and where split datasets go (split_dir). It is a note the project leaves for whoever reads it next: check_project(), a function you will meet after the break; save_output() and its relatives whenever you point them at it; and the containr and submitr sessions after this one. .here is simpler still. It holds nothing; its presence is the message, and after the break it is what lets every path in the analysis start from the same place.

Here’s what a typical _toolero.yml looks like:

# toolero project configuration
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Records the folder structure and naming conventions of a toolero project.
#
# init_project() writes this file to the project root as _toolero.yml after
# resolving the folder set. It records the RESOLVED structure, never the
# inputs that produced it, so a project built from a config file, one built
# with custom_folders, and one built from the defaults all produce the same
# shape of file.
#
# Who reads it:
#   check_project()                  audits the project against this file
#   containr::generate_dockerfile()  learns which folders belong in the image
#   submitr::htc_gen_executable()    learns where the analysis writes output
#
# Commit this file. It describes the project, not your machine.
#
# You can also write one by hand with generate_project_config(), edit it, and
# pass it to init_project(config = ) to drive the structure of a new project.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

schema_version: 1

# One folder per line. Nested paths such as output/figures are supported.
# When this file is passed to init_project(config = ), the list below
# replaces the built-in default set entirely, so list every folder you want
# created.
folders:
  - data-raw
  - data
  - R
  - scripts
  - output/figures
  - output/tables
  - reports
  - assets

# Names the toolero family resolves rather than assumes.
#   output_dir  where the analysis writes artifacts, read by save_output()
#               and generate_manifest()
#   script_dir  where the .R script derived from the .qmd lives
#   split_dir   where write_by_group() writes its per-group subsets
conventions:
  output_dir: output
  script_dir: R
  split_dir: data/jobs

It is fair to ask whether a project that never leaves your laptop needs either file, and the answer is yes, for two reasons. The first is immediate: toolero uses both today, on this laptop, with no container and no cluster in sight. The second is the long game. Together with renv.lock and the record of outputs you’ll meet after the break, these files describe what the project is, what it needs, and what it produces. That description is exactly what the family’s planned fourth package, encapsulr, is being designed to assemble into a self-describing research object: the analysis, its data, its software environment, and the provenance tying them together, packaged so it can be archived with a paper, handed to a reviewer, or deposited in a repository. None of that requires a cluster. A project started this way today will be ready for that step without being rebuilt.

1.6.1 Literate programming, and why a .qmd is where we should start

create_qmd() is the second piece of toolero we are exploring today, and I want to pause on why before showing how. A literate document intertwines narrative, code, and results in one file, rendered in the order a reader would want to encounter them. It is not a script with comments bolted on, and not a write-up that quotes code as an afterthought. The document doesn’t just produce the analysis; it is the analysis, in the same sense that a lab notebook is the record of an experiment rather than a summary of one written afterward.

I am going to state the rest of the case as a claim and leave it untested for now: that for most projects the first file you create should be a .qmd, not an .R script. (I know the instinct runs the other way: a script is smaller, it is what most of us learned first, and a .qmd can feel like ceremony for a figure that took five minutes.) Claims in this session get tested against what happens, so we will come back to this one after the break, with the results of Task 4 in hand.

CautionShow me the call 
create_qmd(
  path             = "~/Documents/palmer-morphometrics",
  filename         = "reports/morphometrics-analysis.qmd",
  header_defaults  = "~/profile.yml",
  use_purl         = TRUE,
  include_examples = FALSE
)

path is the project, and filename says where inside it the document goes. The document lands in reports/, not the project root, and that choice matters in Part Two. include_examples = FALSE gives a clean document with only a header, ready for your own code.

1.6.2 A personal profile, live

header_defaults points at a small personal file holding your name, email, ORCID, institutional affiliation, and whatever else you find yourself retyping into every document’s header. You don’t have to write it from scratch; generate_profile() writes a commented template for you to fill in once, in your home directory by default:

generate_profile("profile.yml")

The part you edit looks like this:

author:
  - name: "Erwin Lares"
    affiliation: "Research Cyberinfrastructure (RCI), Division of Information Technology, UW-Madison"
    orcid: "0000-0002-3284-828X"
    email: "erwin.lares@wisc.edu"

create_qmd() reads this and writes it straight into the new document’s YAML header. The profile can carry document preferences too (a table of contents, embed-resources: true, and so on), so every new document starts the way you like them. It’s a small thing, a header you didn’t have to retype, but it’s the same instinct as init_project()’s folder defaults: a decision you’d otherwise make identically, by hand, every single time, now made once and reused. (If you’ve seen older material that calls this argument yaml_data, that is the same thing under its previous name; it still works, with a deprecation warning, until toolero 0.7.0.)

1.6.3 The purl hook, in one paragraph

With use_purl = TRUE, create_qmd() also stamps purl: true into the document’s header and wires up a _quarto.yml post-render hook that runs a small script, R/purl.R, every time the document renders. The hook writes the document’s code chunks out as a plain .R script under R/, mirroring where the document lives: reports/morphometrics-analysis.qmd becomes R/reports/morphometrics-analysis.R. Why anyone would want a plain script next to a document they have just heard argued for is the question for the second half of the session, and I will answer it then. For now, you have one job: after you render in Task 3, check that the script appeared.

1.7 Task 3: start over, the toolero way

Now do what you did in Task 2, but with toolero:

  1. Run init_project() to create a fresh project for the morphometrics analysis, and open it from the menu: File > Open Project in RStudio, or File > Open Folder in Positron. (2) Copy the packages you need into the new project’s library with renv::hydrate(). (3) Run create_qmd() to scaffold reports/morphometrics-analysis.qmd, with use_purl = TRUE. (4) Copy palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv into data-raw/. (5) Move your Task 1 figure code into the document, render it once, and run renv::snapshot(). You have about ten minutes.

Opening the new project replaces your current window instead of adding a second one. That is on purpose: from here on you work in a single session, and this lesson stays open in your browser.

CautionShow me the call

From inside the new project, where path can stay at its default of ".":

renv::hydrate(packages = c("toolero", "readr", "ggplot2", "rmarkdown"))

toolero::create_qmd(
  filename         = "reports/morphometrics-analysis.qmd",
  use_purl         = TRUE,
  include_examples = FALSE
)

# ...paste your Task 1 code into a code chunk inside the document, render it, then:
renv::snapshot()

The new project starts with an empty package library, and renv keeps the packages you installed before today out of sight while you work inside it. renv::hydrate() copies the ones you name from the library you already have, so nothing is downloaded twice. (Called with no packages, it copies whatever the project’s code uses, and a brand-new project has no code yet.) rmarkdown is on the list because Quarto needs it to render a document with R code in it.

renv::snapshot() writes renv.lock, the record of which packages (and which versions) this analysis actually used. It’s the file the containr session reads.

2 Part Two: When the Document Has to Run More Than One Way

2.1 Framing: one document, two ways to run it

So far, morphometrics-analysis.qmd has only ever been run one way: however you personally happened to build and check it in Task 3. In practice, the same document tends to get run at least two different ways over its life. You step through its chunks interactively in RStudio while you’re working on it, and you call quarto render when you want the finished report. Those two modes don’t always agree on where “here” is on disk, which matters quite a bit for a line of code that says read_csv("palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv") and nothing more specific than that.

2.2 Task 4: run it every way, then break it on purpose

Maris’s grant is funded, and a collaborator at another university now wants to rerun the analysis on her own laptop. Before you hand it over, you want to be sure the document holds up. There is no new data this time; the thing under test is morphometrics-analysis.qmd itself. You have about eight minutes.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio, Session > Restart R). Then run the chunks one at a time, from the top, until the figure appears. Note anything you had to change for that to work.
  2. Render the document. Does it find the data? Is the figure the same?
  3. Now break it on purpose. Put a # in front of the one line that reads the CSV (the penguins <- read_csv(...) line, and nothing else). Run the plot chunk by itself. Does a figure still appear?
  4. Render again. What happens?

When you are done, remove the # so the document is whole again.

2.3 Poll 3

Please answer the following poll:
https://go.wisc.edu/eq94i1

  1. When you ran the chunks one at a time, did the document find its data without any change from what worked when you hit Render? (Yes / No, I had to change something / Didn’t try both)
  2. With the read line commented out, did the plot chunk still draw the figure when you ran it by hand? (Yes / No)
  3. And when you rendered with the line commented out? (It failed / It worked anyway / Didn’t get to try)
  4. Before you tried steps 3 and 4, did you expect the render to fail? (Yes / No / Not sure)

2.3.1 Debrief

This is the same problem from a different angle. Last time, the issue was whether your project structure would hold up under scrutiny. This time, it’s whether your document holds up when it runs somewhere other than the session you built it in: whether it agrees with itself about where “here” is, and whether it quietly depends on anything that only exists in your session.

2.4 Why the document comes first

Before the break I made a claim and left it hanging: that for most projects the first file you create should be a .qmd, not an .R script. Task 4 was the test, and the evidence is on your screens.

Recall what you all saw. You commented out the line that reads the data, and the plot chunk still drew the figure, because an object called penguins was sitting in your session, left behind by the very line you had just removed. Nothing failed. Nothing warned. (Question 4 of Poll 3 asked who saw that coming.) The render could not have made that mistake. quarto render starts a fresh R session and runs the document from the first line to the last, so every object the document uses has to be created by the document itself, in the order it appears. In other words, a successful render is a small proof that the analysis can be rebuilt from nothing. Stepping through code at the console never has to prove that, and a script you have been running line by line all afternoon is exactly the kind of thing that is likely to introduce errors.

Two more reasons are visible in today’s work. The first is the one from Poll 1: when someone else opens your folder, a document tells them what the analysis is for, what it shows, and how it got there, in one place and in the order a reader wants it. A script with comments leaves most of that to the reader. The second is that a document’s header can state what the analysis takes in. The params: block you are about to use is the document saying, in writing, “give me an input file,” which is why a collaborator can point the same document at her own copy of the data without editing the code.

None of this makes scripts bad, and I would not want you to leave with that impression. It makes a document the better place to work: to explore, to explain, to check. Whether it is also the best thing to run is a separate question, and the answer is not always yes.

2.5 And yet: why a machine wants a script

Push the scenario one step further:

Six months from now, this analysis needs to run as part of a larger, automated pipeline: something that starts a job on a machine you will never log into, with no human at the Render button and no one to read the result. You already have a plain script for it. It appeared in R/reports/ when you rendered in Task 3, and I owe you an explanation of where it came from.

Run it from a terminal:

Rscript R/reports/morphometrics-analysis.R

There’s now a third context, with its own notion of “here”: typically wherever the terminal happened to be sitting when you launched it, which may not match either of the first two. We will fix that shortly. First, the question I promised: why would a pipeline run a script when we have just spent a few minutes arguing for the document?

I can give three reasons. None of them is overwhelming for one small analysis, and all of them multiply when a job runs hundreds of times on machines you cannot see. The first is fewer moving parts. Rscript needs R and your packages. Rendering also needs Quarto, and whatever Quarto calls on to do its work, installed and working on the node, and every extra tool is one more thing that has to be present on a machine you can’t log into. (The next session makes this concrete: everything a job needs goes into a container image, so every extra tool is another layer in it.) The second is that there is no reader. The deliverable of an unattended job is files on disk and an answer to “did it work.” A rendered report is something nobody will open at 2 a.m., and producing it costs time and can fail for reasons unrelated to your analysis, for instance, a stylesheet path. The third is that the command line is the interface a scheduler speaks. Rscript script.R some-file.csv is about as small an interface as exists, and every job scheduler already knows how to launch it. (Quarto can take parameters and report failure too, so this is a matter of weight, not of capability.)

So the document is where you work, and a script is what a machine runs. That leaves a question, and it is the one the sixth item in Poll 1 asked: if both exist, who keeps them in sync?

2.6 The purl hook: one source, two artifacts

The answer is neither to choose nor to maintain both. It is to write one and generate the other, and that is the job of the hook you switched on with use_purl = TRUE. The .qmd is the file you edit. Every time it renders, the post-render hook runs R/purl.R, which extracts the document’s code into its .R twin. Nobody types the script, so nobody can forget to update it. Humans read documents, machines run scripts, and nobody maintains both.

The second half of the lab below uses a function you haven’t met yet. check_project() audits a project. It walks through a checklist of what a well-kept project should have (the folders, renv.lock, git, and a few more) and prints one row per item, saying whether it passed. We will read the whole report at the end of the day. For now, one row matters: for every document marked purl: true, check_project() checks that its script exists and that the script is newer than the document.

Lab (three minutes). In your morphometrics-analysis.qmd, change the plot’s title and render. Open R/reports/morphometrics-analysis.R and find the new title: you never touched that file. Then change the title once more and, this time, save but do not render. Run check_project() from the project root and find the row for your document.

The second half of the lab is where the limit shows. The hook fires when the document renders, so if you edit and forget to render, the script is one edit behind, and a pipeline that runs it will run yesterday’s analysis without a word of complaint. check_project() is the safety net: it compares the two files and names the script as stale. The other limit runs the opposite way. The .R is generated, so if you edit it by hand, your edit is overwritten at the next render. The working rule fits in one line: edit the .qmd, render, and treat the .R as output. Follow it and the two files cannot drift apart in content. (That is “by construction,” with one asterisk, and the asterisk is the render.)

If forgetting to render worries you, there are a few things you can do to make it less likely. In RStudio or Positron you can tick the Render on Save checkbox yourself. You can also ask for it in the document’s front matter and, if you want it for every document in the project, in _quarto.yml. I haven’t decided one way or another whether I want toolero to make that choice for you, but I am leaning toward making it visible at the very least.

editor:
  render-on-save: true

That settles drift in content. Drift in behavior is a different problem, and Task 4 and the Rscript demo already showed where it comes from: the document and its script run in three different places, and each has its own idea of where “here” is. Three contexts, one read call. That is the next problem toolero offers a solution for.

2.7 toolero’s answer: resolve_input_path()

resolve_input_path() takes one argument per context, interactive, quarto, and rscript, works out at runtime which of the three it is currently in, and returns the path that context should use. One function call, one document, no separately maintained versions.

CautionShow me the call 
library(toolero)

input_file <- resolve_input_path(
  interactive = "data-raw/palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv"
)

penguins <- read_csv(input_file)

Only the interactive argument is spelled out, because the other two have defaults that already do the right thing. Under quarto render, the quarto argument falls back to a document parameter, params$input_file. That requires a params: entry in the document’s YAML header:

params:
  input_file: "data-raw/palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv"

Notice that both paths are spelled the same way, from the project root, even though quarto render runs the document from reports/. In the interactive and Quarto contexts, resolve_input_path() reads a relative path from the project root, the folder marked by the .here file init_project() wrote, not from wherever the code happens to be running. That is the whole disagreement from Part Two’s opening, removed at the source.

Under Rscript, the rscript argument falls back to the first thing typed after the script’s name on the command line:

Rscript R/reports/morphometrics-analysis.R data-raw/palmer-morphometrics-2024.csv

This is a brief, deliberate use of Quarto parameters, not a full detour into parameterized rendering. The point to land is narrower: once the document knows which context it’s in, each context can resolve its input the way that context expects, and the same .qmd, along with its purl-generated .R twin, runs correctly whether it’s rendered, stepped through interactively, or called from a shell script at 2 a.m. with nobody watching.

Two properties of resolve_input_path() separate it from writing the same logic by hand. First, only the argument for the current context is ever evaluated. A document with no params: block still runs from Rscript, and if you render it anyway, you get a message pointing at the missing YAML entry rather than R’s object 'params' not found. Second, by default it checks that the file it resolved actually exists (must_exist = TRUE) and says which context it was in when it didn’t, which turns “where is here?” from a guessing game into one line of explanation.

The input is not the only path in the document, though. Anything the analysis writes has the same problem in reverse: a bare ggsave("output/figures/bill.png") works interactively from the project root and, under quarto render, quietly creates reports/output/ instead. The fix is the same rule, applied to every other path in your code: start at the project root, and write it with here::here(), which finds the same .here file.

ggsave(here::here("output", "figures", "bill-morphometrics.png"), bill_plot)

On a cluster, where there is no project root to find, here::here() falls back to the job’s working directory, which is where the results need to land anyway. The one exception is the paths in the document’s own YAML header, such as a stylesheet: Quarto resolves those from the document itself, so they stay relative to reports/.

This is the other half of the loop the purl hook opened. The hook kept the document and its script from drifting apart in content; resolve_input_path() keeps them from needing to drift apart in behavior either, across however many contexts they end up running in.

3 Part Three: From One Figure to a Whole Analysis

3.1 Leaving a record, and meeting minimal-project.qmd

Your document draws one figure. That was the right size for Maris’s first favor, but it is not the size of most real analyses. A typical analysis, in almost any discipline, does about the same handful of things: it loads some data and checks what came through, makes a figure or two, summarizes something, fits a model, and writes the results somewhere a collaborator or a manuscript can find them. The figure from Task 1 is one of those jobs. For authenticity’s sake, we’ll work with a more comprehensive document, one that better reflects the realities of research.

minimal-project.qmd is the smallest document I could write that does all of them. It picks up the Sphen Lab story where we left it: after the first figure, the obvious next asks are a summary of flipper length by species and a model relating flipper length to body mass, and Maris will almost certainly want every result saved. The document runs in four stages: load the observations and check what came through, draw the bill figure (yours, again), summarize flipper length by species, and fit the small model. It is deliberately modest, so that it can stand in for whatever your own analysis does. The data would differ; the kinds of work would not.

It is also the document we carry through the next two sessions. In the next one it goes into a container, and in the one after that it goes to a cluster, and it was written to survive both trips: every path in it starts at the project root, it finds its input with resolve_input_path(), it writes everything under output/, and it ends by recording what it wrote. Let’s stop on that last habit.

There is one question left from the 2 a.m. scenario, and it is the one people usually ask too late. When the document ran with nobody watching, what did it actually produce? Did every file get written, or did the third figure fail halfway through? A folder of outputs cannot tell you which of its files are from tonight’s run and which are left over from last week’s.

save_output() answers that by wrapping whatever function writes the file. It calls the writer for you, and on the way it appends a line to output/accumulator.csv: the file, the kind of object, the function that wrote it, whether the write succeeded (and the error, if it did not), and an optional note. At the end of the document, generate_manifest() collapses those lines into the output record, output/project-manifest.json, one entry per file, along with the git commit the document was run from.

CautionShow me the call 
# ggsave() takes the file name first and the plot second, the reverse of
# the order save_output() passes them in, so it needs a small wrapper.
save_plot <- function(object, file_path, ...) {
  ggplot2::ggsave(filename = file_path, plot = object, ...)
}

save_output(
  bill_plot,
  here::here("output", "figures", "bill-morphometrics.png"),
  .f     = save_plot,
  width  = 7,
  height = 5,
  dpi    = 300,
  note   = "The appendix figure"
)

And as the document’s last chunk:

generate_manifest(overwrite = TRUE)

overwrite = TRUE because every render writes a fresh record. Then, from the console:

read_output_records()

read_output_records() reads the record back as a table, one row per file: file_path, function_used, status, note, and the facts about the run as a whole, commit among them. A table is something you can filter (which writes failed?) or put straight into the report, which is what minimal-project.qmd does in its last section, in place of a list of files someone would have to keep by hand.

You will not build this document today, and you will not have to. I will give you the whole project it lives in, minimal-project-day2.zip, as the starting point for the next session. Compare it with yours when you have it: yours draws one figure, and this one draws that figure too, then summarizes, models, and saves. It is today’s lesson with a few more jobs and nothing else new. If you want a record in your own document, adding save_output() calls and a closing generate_manifest() is the same change we just looked at, and nothing in the next session depends on it.

3.2 Retrofitting: what the project already knows

I hope that I have managed to convince you by now that toolero’s init_project() and create_qmd() reduce much of the friction we encounter in our day-to-day work, as well as make following best practices easier to adopt. But what about all the projects you work on that already exist? Sometimes you inherit one, or you’re six months into something that predates this session entirely. Two functions exist specifically for that situation, and you have already met one of them.

Recall the purl lab: check_project() printed a whole report, and we read a single row of it. The rest of that report is the function’s main job. check_project() audits an existing directory, whether one you built by hand or one a labmate handed you, against the same checklist init_project() satisfies automatically: expected folders, an .Rproj file, renv.lock, git, a README, a .gitignore, and the absence of stray session files like .RData or .Rhistory. When the project has a _toolero.yml, check_project() reads the expected folders from it rather than assuming the defaults. The stale-script row from the lab is one more item on the same list. Run it once more on the project you built today:

check_project()

If you re-rendered your document in the last segment, the row for it should now pass, since the script caught up the moment you rendered. Read the rest of the report: it is the checklist init_project() satisfied for you without being asked. Pointed at a project that did not start this way, the same report becomes a to-do list.

qmd_to_r() is the retrofit counterpart to the purl hook from Part One. It extracts the R code from any .qmd, including one that was never created with create_qmd() in the first place, into a standalone .R script.

qmd_to_r(input = "inherited-analysis.qmd", output = "R/inherited-analysis.R")

A documentation argument controls how much commentary survives the extraction: chunk labels only (the default), full roxygen-style blocks, or bare code with nothing else. Mention it if the extracted script is headed somewhere that cares about it, like a shared scripts folder with its own conventions.

A few smaller generators round out the record-keeping side of a project, each one a single call that writes a file you’d otherwise start from a blank page: generate_citation() writes a CITATION.cff, reusing the profile from Part One; generate_license() writes a LICENSE; and generate_data_doc() writes a short documentation stub for one dataset.

Finally, a pointer rather than a demo: when an analysis needs to run separately across subsets of the data (one model per species, say, rather than one model against everything at once), write_by_group() and run_by_group() are the pair that handles it, splitting the data once and applying a function to each piece. Out of scope for today, but it will be there the day this project needs it, and it’s the starting point of the submitr session.

3.3 Wrap-up

Two kinds of friction turned up today. The first was loud: setting up a folder, renv, and git by hand, under the vague suspicion that the result might not hold up. init_project() and create_qmd() removed it without asking you to predict in advance which projects deserve the effort. The second was quieter, and only appeared once the same analysis had to run in more than one place. resolve_input_path() and here::here() removed the disagreement about where “here” is, the purl hook removed the need to maintain a document and a script by hand, and save_output() made sure the analysis can say afterwards what it did. In every case the fix was the same in spirit: a decision you’d otherwise have to get right identically every time, replaced by one you make once.

If I had to compress the day into a sentence, it would be the one from the middle of the session: work in a document, run a script, and never maintain both by hand.

That sentence is also the bridge to the next session. Everything we built today makes the analysis easy to run in the places you control, and minimal-project.qmd, the document you saw a few minutes ago, is what we carry forward. It has a problem yours does not have yet: it uses more packages than you did (besides what you used today, it loads dplyr, gt, and broom), and renv.lock records all of them while recording nothing about what those packages need from the machine underneath. The containr session takes that lockfile and builds an environment around it, so the same script runs wherever it lands, and the session after that sends it to a cluster. The thread running through all three is the one you just pulled on: the decision made once, made visible, recorded somewhere durable, and reused.

The full function reference, including a few tools not covered today (arborize(), generate_kb_xml(), read_clean_csv(), and write_clean_csv()), is documented at github.com/erwinlares/toolero.
